notes.h: Size and growth of Brazil's population
notes.b: Brazil is one of the most populous countries in the world, but its growth has slowed sharply. The latest count comes from the 2022 Census.
points: The 2022 Census counted about 203 million people, up from about 191 million in the 2010 Census.
Annual growth between 2010 and 2022 was only about 0.5 percent, the slowest ever recorded in Brazil, so the population is close to levelling off.
The census was due in 2020 but was delayed until 2022, so the 2022 Census is Brazil's latest, not a 2020 census.
notes.tip: Label population figures as 2022 Census and religion figures as 2010 Census. Never call the latest census the 2020 census.

notes.b: The demographic transition is the shift from high birth and death rates to low ones as a country develops. Brazil has moved through it quickly since the mid-20th century.
points: Death rates fell from the mid-20th century because of vaccination, clean water and better medicine, while birth rates stayed high, so the population grew fast.
Fertility then collapsed, from about 6 children per woman in 1960 to about 1.6 in the early 2020s, which is below the replacement level of 2.1 (the level needed to keep numbers steady).
Urbanisation lowered fertility, because children cost more to raise in cities and are no longer needed as farm labour.
Women's education and paid work, and wider use of contraception, let women choose smaller families.
notes.tip: For a population distribution question, give no more than one sentence on fertility. Save the detail for a question on population dynamics.

notes.b: Falling fertility has changed the shape of the population pyramid (a chart of the share of people at each age). Brazil is ageing.
points: The base of the pyramid is shrinking, because fewer children are being born each year.
Life expectancy is about 76 years (early 2020s), so more people reach old age and the older age groups are growing.
Old-age dependency is rising, which means fewer workers support each retired person.
A pension reform in 2019 raised the retirement age to ease the cost of pensions.

notes.b: Brazil's people are spread very unevenly. Comparing the five macro-regions shows where most of them live.
points: The 2022 Census gave these shares of the population: Southeast about 42 percent, Northeast about 27 percent, South about 15 percent, North about 8.5 percent and Centre-West about 8 percent.
The North covers about 45 percent of Brazil's area but holds only about 8.5 percent of its people, which shows how thinly the Amazon is settled.
National density in 2022 was about 24 people per km2, low for a big country because so much of the interior is empty.
In general the population is dense along the coast and in the Southeast, and sparse in the Amazon and the interior.
notes.tip: Population distribution is a frequent Higher Level question. Use these shares and density figures, and explain dense and sparse areas with both physical and human factors.

notes.h: Dense areas: the Southeast and the cities
notes.b: The densest part of Brazil is the Southeast, where good land, a mild climate and jobs come together.
points: Colonial settlement came from the sea, so people clustered near ports; the saying is that Brazilians were 'clinging to the coast like crabs'.
The Southeast plateau has a cooler highland climate, with São Paulo cooler than Rio de Janeiro on the coast, which made it pleasant and healthy to settle.
Fertile terra roxa (deep red soil formed from basalt) supported the coffee boom and drew farm workers and then their families.
The industrial jobs and services of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte keep pulling migrants, so the cities have grown very large.
São Paulo state holds about 44 million people (2022 Census), the most populous state in Brazil.

notes.h: Dense areas: the coast and the sugar coast
notes.b: The Atlantic coast is dense because the Portuguese arrived by sea and found rich farmland and good harbours there.
points: Ports such as Santos and Salvador gave trade routes to Portugal, so towns grew where ships could land.
On the humid coastal strip of the Northeast, the Zona da Mata around Recife and Salvador, massapê (dark, clay-rich, fertile soil) supported sugar plantations.
The sugar plantations needed large workforces, first enslaved Africans and later poor rural families, so this strip filled with people early.
Rain from the south-east trade winds is heavy on the coast, so water supply for crops and towns is reliable, unlike the dry interior.

notes.b: Large parts of the North have very few people. The Amazon basin makes everyday life and farming hard.
points: The dense rainforest is hard to clear and travel through, and there are few roads, so access is poor.
Heat and humidity all year, with tropical disease, make settlement unattractive for many people.
Most Amazon soils are latosols (deep, leached, acidic and low in nutrients), so cleared land gives poor crops after a few years.
Amazonas state has a density under 3 people per km2 (2022 Census), and Roraima is the least populous state.
notes.tip: Don't call Amazon soils fertile. The exceptions are the várzea (floodplain soils) and terra preta, which are small areas.

notes.h: Sparse areas: the Centre-West and the sertão
notes.b: Two more regions are thinly settled for different reasons: one because of isolation, the other because of drought.
points: The Centre-West was isolated for centuries, far from the coast and ports, with no roads, so few settlers went there before Brasília was built in 1960.
The sertão (the dry interior of the Northeast) is semi-arid, with roughly 250 to 800 mm of rain a year that varies greatly from year to year.
Droughts in the sertão, such as the severe one from 2012 to 2017, destroy crops and push people out, so the region has lost many people.
Thin, stony sertão soils erode easily, so farming there gives little income to support large numbers.

notes.h: Density contrast: São Paulo and Amazonas
notes.b: A direct comparison of two states is a strong way to finish a distribution answer.
points: São Paulo state has about 44 million people (2022 Census) at a density of about 180 per km2.
Amazonas state has a density under 3 per km2, so São Paulo is around sixty times denser.
The contrast comes from the factors above: São Paulo has a plateau climate, fertile soil, ports, industry and services, while Amazonas has forest, heat, poor soils and few roads.

notes.h: Policies to move people inland: Brasília and the March to the West
notes.b: Because so many people lived on the coast, governments tried to open up the empty interior.
points: Brasília, the new capital, was inaugurated on 21 April 1960 in the centre of the country to draw people and investment inland.
The 'March to the West' was the drive to settle the Centre-West, and the new capital and roads made it possible.
The Centre-West later became the soya frontier, so the interior now holds more people and farms than before Brasília.
notes.tip: The capital is Brasília, not Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo. Rio was the capital until 1960.

notes.h: Colonising the Amazon: Trans-Amazonian Highway and Rondônia
notes.b: From 1970 the government tried to settle the Amazon, but many schemes failed.
points: The Programme of National Integration (1970) built the Trans-Amazonian Highway, opened in 1972, using the slogan 'a land without people for people without land'.
INCRA (the National Institute for Colonisation and Agrarian Reform, 1970) gave plots of land to settlers.
In the 1980s the Polonoroeste programme settled families in Rondônia along the BR-364 road.
Many schemes failed because the poor soils gave low yields and the settlers lived far from markets, so many farmers sold up or moved on.

notes.b: Internal migration is movement within Brazil. The biggest flow has been from the Northeast to the Southeast.
points: Nordestinos (migrants from the Northeast) moved from the sertão to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, mainly from the 1950s to the 1980s.
Push factors: drought, poverty and the concentration of land in few hands left many with no work.
Pull factors: factory jobs, for example in the ABC car plants near São Paulo, offered wages and a chance of a better life.
More recently, people have moved to the Centre-West farm frontier, and some have returned to the Northeast.

notes.b: Brazil's people came from many places. Immigration shaped the population and the economy.
points: Portuguese settlers arrived from 1500 and set up the colony.
About 4 to 5 million enslaved Africans were brought to Brazil, more than to any other country, to work sugar, gold and coffee.
Italian and German immigrants came, especially to São Paulo and the South, as coffee and farm labour.
Japanese immigration began in 1908 with the ship Kasato Maru; Brazil has the largest population of Japanese descent outside Japan, centred on São Paulo.
Recent arrivals include Venezuelans, received at Pacaraima in Roraima under Operation Welcome (2018), and people from Haiti.

notes.b: Brazil abolished slavery late, and some Brazilians now leave to work abroad.
points: Slavery was abolished on 13 May 1888, so Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end it.
Brazilians have emigrated to the USA, Portugal, Japan and Ireland.
In Ireland, a Brazilian community grew in Gort, Co. Galway, from the late 1990s through meat-plant work, and there is another in Dublin.
About 27,000 Brazilian citizens lived in Ireland in the 2022 Census of Ireland.

notes.b: Brazil's population is a mixture of Indigenous peoples, Portuguese colonists, enslaved Africans and later immigrants. Census categories are based on how people describe themselves.
points: In the 2022 Census, pardo (mixed) was the largest group at about 45 percent, and it was the largest for the first time since 1991.
White (branco) was about 44 percent and Black (preto) about 10 percent.
Indigenous and Asian (amarelo) people were each under 1 percent.
This mix comes from colonisation, the slave trade and later immigration from Europe and Japan.

notes.b: Brazil's first peoples live in hundreds of groups. They face pressure on their land.
points: The Indigenous population was about 1.7 million in the 2022 Census, in hundreds of ethnic groups.
Examples are the Yanomami (Roraima and Amazonas), the Kayapó (Pará and Mato Grosso) and the Guarani (south and Centre-West).
Demarcated Indigenous lands (areas legally set aside for them) cover about 13 percent of Brazil, mostly in the Amazon.
Mining, ranching and dams threaten these lands; for example, the Kayapó opposed the Belo Monte Dam.

notes.b: Mixing has not meant equality. Colour still follows income in Brazil.
points: Black and pardo Brazilians earn less on average than white Brazilians and are over-represented in favelas.
The idea of 'racial democracy' (that Brazil mixed peoples without racism) is a claim, not reality.
The Law of Quotas (2012) reserves places in federal universities for state-school students, with places for Black, pardo and Indigenous students, to widen access.
notes.tip: Racial democracy is a myth, not a fact. Don't write that Brazil has no racism.

notes.b: Portuguese gives Brazil a single common language across a continental-sized country.
points: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided new lands between Spain and Portugal, and Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, so Portuguese came with colonisation.
Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas and the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world.
Brazil won independence from Portugal in 1822 yet kept the language.
One language unites the country, unlike India, which has many major languages.
notes.tip: Brazilians speak Portuguese, not Spanish. Brazil is surrounded by Spanish-speaking neighbours.

notes.b: Over time, Brazilian Portuguese has drifted away from the Portuguese of Portugal.
points: It differs from European Portuguese in sound and vocabulary.
It took in many Tupi (Indigenous) words, including place names and the names of plants and animals such as jaguar, piranha and tapioca.
It also absorbed words from African languages, brought by enslaved people.

notes.b: Hundreds of Indigenous languages survive, but they are under threat.
points: The 2010 Census recorded 305 Indigenous ethnic groups speaking 274 Indigenous languages, mostly in the Amazon.
Most of these languages are endangered, because speakers are few and children learn Portuguese at school.
In 2002 Nheengatu, Tukano and Baniwa became co-official languages of São Gabriel da Cachoeira (Amazonas), the first municipality to do this.

notes.b: Other languages came with later settlers.
points: Hunsrik (a German dialect) and Talian (an Italian dialect) are spoken in the South, where German and Italian farmers settled.
Japanese is spoken in São Paulo, in districts such as Liberdade, because of Japanese immigration from 1908.
Libras (Brazilian Sign Language) was recognised by law in 2002.

notes.b: Language shapes who Brazil trades with and how easily visitors and firms can do business.
points: Portuguese ties Brazil to Portugal, Angola and Mozambique through the Community of Portuguese Language Countries.
Few Brazilians speak English, a barrier to tourism and global business compared with India.
Brazil's Mercosur neighbours speak Spanish, so language separates it from its trading partners even within the bloc.

notes.b: Brazil has the largest Catholic population of any country, but its religious make-up is changing.
points: In the 2010 Census, Roman Catholic was about 65 percent, evangelical (Protestant, mainly Pentecostal) about 22 percent, no religion about 8 percent and Spiritist about 2 percent.
Catholicism came with Portuguese colonisation and the Jesuit missions (Catholic priests who founded mission settlements).
São Paulo itself was founded as a Jesuit mission on 25 January 1554 by Manuel da Nóbrega and José de Anchieta.
Surveys since 2010 show Catholics falling further and evangelicals rising.
notes.tip: Label these religion figures as 2010 Census, not 2022.

notes.b: Enslaved Africans brought their own beliefs, which blended with the Catholicism they were made to follow.
points: Candomblé (from Yoruba and other West African traditions) and Umbanda are Afro-Brazilian religions.
They show syncretism (the blending of two belief systems), because African spirits were linked with Catholic saints.
They are strongest in Salvador, Bahia, which was a major port of arrival for enslaved people.

notes.b: The religious map is shifting, with social and political effects.
points: Catholicism is declining while Pentecostal churches grow, especially among the urban poor.
The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God was founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977, and the Assemblies of God is the largest Pentecostal denomination.
Evangelicals have gained political power, and there is intolerance against Afro-Brazilian religions.
Brazil has been a secular republic since the 1891 Constitution, so there is no official state religion.

notes.b: Religious events bring money and visitors.
points: Carnival is the festival of the days before Ash Wednesday and Lent (a Catholic season), and it draws huge numbers of tourists and spending, especially in Rio de Janeiro.
The Basilica of Our Lady of Aparecida (São Paulo state) is the shrine of Brazil's patron saint and one of the largest Catholic churches in the world, so it attracts pilgrims.
The Círio de Nazaré procession in Belém each October draws about two million people.
Together these make religious tourism a real source of jobs and income.
notes.tip: Carnival is the festival before Lent, not a harvest festival.

notes.b: Brazil has changed from a rural to an urban country in about seventy years.
points: About 36 percent of people lived in towns in 1950, and about 87 percent do today (2020s).
Rural-urban migration drove this, as people left farms for cities.
Mechanisation of farming cut the need for workers, and land concentration left many with no land.
Drought pushed people from the sertão, while industrial jobs in cities pulled them.

notes.b: A few huge cities dominate, followed by regional capitals.
points: São Paulo (about 11.5 million, and over 20 million in Greater São Paulo) and Rio de Janeiro (about 6.2 million) are the two megacities (2022 Census).
Next come the regional capitals: Brasília about 2.8 million, Fortaleza and Salvador about 2.4 million each, Belo Horizonte about 2.3 million and Manaus about 2.1 million (2022 Census).
The largest city is São Paulo, but the capital is Brasília.
notes.tip: The capital is Brasília. São Paulo is the largest and richest city.

notes.b: São Paulo is Brazil's largest city. Its site, the actual spot where it was built, helped it grow.
points: It sits on the plateau about 800 m above sea level, behind the Serra do Mar escarpment, and about 70 km from the port of Santos.
The Tietê river runs through it and supplied water.
It began as a Jesuit mission, founded on 25 January 1554.
The plateau gives a cooler climate than the coast, and the escarpment kept early settlers safe from the coast, though it also made travel to the port hard.

notes.h: São Paulo: factors in its growth
notes.b: Several factors, one building on the last, made a small mission into a megacity.
points: The coffee boom of the 19th century brought wealth, and the coffee was exported through Santos.
The São Paulo Railway to Santos (1867, British-built) linked the plateau to the port.
Immigrants, including Italians and Japanese (in the district of Liberdade), supplied labour and skills.
Industrialisation followed, with coffee profits funding first factories and then the ABC car plants.
Migrants from the Northeast supplied cheap labour for the factories.
Today São Paulo is Brazil's financial and service capital.
notes.tip: Questions ask for factors that influenced the development of one urban area, or the reasons for its growth. São Paulo is the expected case study, so link each factor to growth.

notes.b: Fast growth outran planning, and the city has serious problems.
points: Favelas (informal, self-built housing) and self-built housing spread on the urban edge, such as Heliópolis, the largest favela, and Paraisópolis beside the wealthy district of Morumbi.
Traffic and air pollution are severe in a city of this size.
The 2014-15 water crisis saw the Cantareira reservoir system fall to a few percent of capacity.
Flooding is a regular problem, and the Tietê is heavily polluted by sewage.
Inequality and crime are widespread.

notes.b: The city and government have tried several responses.
points: The rodízio scheme (1997) bans cars from the central area at rush hours on one weekday, depending on the last digit of the number plate, to cut congestion.
Metro and bus corridors have been built to move people without cars.
Favela upgrading improves existing neighbourhoods instead of clearing them.
Minha Casa Minha Vida ('My House, My Life', 2009) is a social housing programme.

notes.b: Rio is the second megacity and was Brazil's capital for almost two centuries.
points: Its site is on Guanabara Bay between mountains and sea, which gives it a famous setting and a good harbour.
It was the capital from 1763 to 1960, before Brasília.
Its economy rests on its port, tourism and oil services.
Hillside favelas such as Rocinha are among Brazil's largest, and the steep slopes make landslides a risk, as in the mountain region in 2011.
Pacifying Police Units (UPPs) began in 2008 to bring security to favelas.

notes.b: Brasília was built from nothing to open the interior.
points: It was inaugurated on 21 April 1960 as the capital.
Lúcio Costa drew the Pilot Plan, shaped like an aeroplane or bird, and Oscar Niemeyer designed the buildings.
It was built to open the interior of the country to settlement.
Unplanned satellite cities such as Ceilândia (towns outside the plan for workers) grew up, which shows segregation between planned and unplanned areas.

notes.b: Two smaller cases show how one city grew from a river and another from planning.
points: Manaus is a river port in the heart of the Amazon, which ocean ships can reach.
Rubber wealth built the Teatro Amazonas, and the Free Trade Zone revived the city after the boom.
Growth has cleared nearby forest.
Curitiba is a model of planning: its bus rapid transit began in 1974, it has parks on flood-prone land, and it runs recycling schemes.

notes.b: Problems found across Brazilian cities have a common root in rapid migration.
points: About 16 million people, about 8 percent of the population, live in favelas and urban communities (2022 Census).
Many people work in the informal economy (jobs without contracts or tax), so their income is low and insecure.
Poor sanitation affects areas with no sewers or piped water.
Violence is common, and wealthy people live in gated communities beside favelas.
notes.tip: Don't say all urban poor live in favelas, and don't give a population for any single favela.

notes.b: Rural Brazil is a small and shrinking share of the population, and it has serious problems.
points: The rural population is concentrated in the Northeast and the North.
Poverty is worst in the Northeast sertão, where drought destroys crops.
Land is concentrated in few hands, so many families are landless, and there is rural violence over land.
Services such as water, electricity, health and schools are poor, so young people leave.

notes.b: The unfair division of land is the central rural issue.
points: The MST (Landless Rural Workers' Movement, founded 1984) occupies unused estates to press for redistribution (sharing the land more fairly).
INCRA runs official settlements, but progress is slow and contested.
The MST is a movement, not a government body.
notes.tip: The MST is a movement, not a government body, and Bolsa Família is a cash scheme, not land reform.

notes.b: The government has tried to reduce rural poverty with payments and services.
points: Bolsa Família (2003) pays cash on condition that children attend school and are vaccinated; it was relaunched in 2023, reaching about 20 million families.
Fome Zero ('Zero Hunger', 2003) fought hunger, and Brazil left the UN Hunger Map in 2014.
One Million Cisterns (from 2003, run with the civil-society network ASA) provides rainwater tanks in the sertão.
Luz para Todos ('Light for All', 2003) brought electricity to rural homes.
Credit for family farms and SUDENE support the Northeast.
notes.tip: Bolsa Família is a cash-transfer scheme, not land reform.

notes.h: Contrasting outcomes: Mato Grosso and the sertão
notes.b: Two rural areas show how human, economic and physical processes interact.
points: Mato Grosso is Brazil's leading soya state, where reliable summer rain, flat land and liming (adding crushed limestone to acidic soil) support agribusiness boom towns.
The sertão is poor because of low, unreliable rain, thin soils and unequal land ownership.
The gap shows that farming wealth depends on technology, markets and land ownership as well as climate and soil.

notes.b: Brazil is divided into a richer core and a poorer periphery, which shows human, economic and physical processes working together.
points: The core is the Southeast and the South, where industry, ports and services are concentrated; the periphery is the Northeast and North.
The Federal District and São Paulo have the highest income per person, while Maranhão and Piauí in the Northeast are among the poorest states.

The causes are rooted in climate (drought in the sertão), soils, colonial history (the sugar coast was left behind when coffee and then industry moved south) and the concentration of industry in São Paulo.
Responses include SUDENE (1959, for the Northeast), SUDAM (1966, for the Amazon) and the Manaus Free Trade Zone (1967).
Brazil is among the most unequal countries in the world.
notes.tip: Examiners expect the human processes to be tied to economic and physical ones, and this block is the way to do it.

notes.b: Physical, economic and human processes in Brazil are linked in chains, and these make strong conclusions.
points: Coffee on terra roxa brought wealth, which funded São Paulo industry, which drew migrants from the drought-hit sertão and led to favelas.
Cerrado liming and EMBRAPA research led to a soya boom, which needed the BR-163 road and northern ports and put pressure on the Amazon.
Rainfall and plateau rivers give hydroelectricity, which powers industry.
Portuguese colonisation left Brazil with its language, its religion and an export economy.
notes.tip: For a Higher Level question on the impact of human processes on development, pick two processes and link each to economic and physical processes.

keyTerms: Nordestino
A migrant from the Northeast of Brazil, especially one who moved from the sertão to São Paulo or Rio de Janeiro.
Favela
An informal, self-built urban settlement, often on steep hills or the urban edge, with poor services.
Pardo
The Brazilian census category for people of mixed ancestry, the largest group in the 2022 Census at about 45 percent.
Syncretism
The blending of two belief systems, as when Candomblé joins West African spirits to Catholic saints.
Candomblé
An Afro-Brazilian religion from Yoruba and other West African traditions, strongest in Salvador, Bahia.
Bolsa Família
A cash-transfer scheme begun in 2003 that pays families on condition that children attend school and are vaccinated.
Demographic transition as applied to Brazil
Death rates fell from the mid-20th century while births stayed high, then fertility fell from about 6 children per woman in 1960 to about 1.6.
Rodízio
São Paulo's 1997 scheme that bans cars from the central area at rush hours on one weekday, by the last digit of the number plate.
Satellite city
A town outside a planned city, such as Ceilândia near Brasília, that houses workers the plan did not provide for.
Racial democracy
The claim that Brazil mixed its peoples without racism; in reality Black and pardo Brazilians earn less.
MST
The Landless Rural Workers' Movement, founded in 1984, which occupies unused estates to press for land redistribution.
Sertão
The dry, semi-arid interior of the Northeast, which has low and unreliable rain and is prone to drought.

About 203 million in the 2022 Census, growing about 0.5 percent a year since 2010, the slowest ever recorded.
Regional shares of population, 2022 Census
Southeast about 42 percent, Northeast about 27 percent, South about 15 percent, North about 8.5 percent, Centre-West about 8 percent.
São Paulo state against Amazonas: density
São Paulo has about 44 million people at about 180 per km2; Amazonas has under 3 per km2.
Why the Amazon is sparsely populated
Dense forest, heat and humidity, leached soils, disease and poor access.

About 6 children per woman in 1960 down to about 1.6 in the early 2020s, below the replacement level of 2.1.

Pardo about 45 percent, white about 44 percent, Black about 10 percent, Indigenous and Asian each under 1 percent.
Religion in the 2010 Census
Roman Catholic about 65 percent, evangelical about 22 percent, no religion about 8 percent, Spiritist about 2 percent.
Languages of Brazil: three examples
Portuguese is the national language; Indigenous languages such as Nheengatu are co-official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira; Hunsrik and Talian are spoken in the South.
São Paulo: founding and growth
Founded by Jesuits on 25 January 1554, it grew through coffee, the railway to Santos in 1867, immigration and industry.
São Paulo: four problems
Favelas such as Heliópolis, traffic and air pollution, the 2014-15 water crisis, and flooding and inequality.
Urban share of Brazil's people
About 36 percent in 1950 and about 87 percent in the 2020s.
Brasília: who planned it and when
Inaugurated on 21 April 1960, planned by Lúcio Costa with buildings by Oscar Niemeyer.
Rural development schemes since 2003
Bolsa Família, One Million Cisterns, Luz para Todos and Fome Zero.
Policies to move people inland
Brasília (1960), the March to the West, the Trans-Amazonian Highway (1970s) and Rondônia along the BR-364 (1980s).

questions.prompt: Account for the distribution of population in Brazil.
questions.model: Brazil's overall density is low, about 24 people per km2 (2022 Census), because the population of about 203 million is very unevenly spread. The 2022 Census shows the Southeast has about 42 percent of the population, the Northeast about 27 percent, the South about 15 percent, the North about 8.5 percent and the Centre-West about 8 percent. The North covers about 45 percent of the area but holds only about 8.5 percent of the people. Dense areas first. The Southeast is densest, because the plateau climate is cooler than the coast and fertile terra roxa from basalt supported the coffee boom. Its industrial jobs in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte, and its services, keep drawing migrants, so São Paulo state has about 44 million people. The coast is dense because colonial settlement came from the sea, with ports such as Santos and Salvador. On the Northeast sugar coast, the Zona da Mata, fertile massapê soils and reliable rain from the trade winds supported plantations that needed large workforces. Cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador and Fortaleza are dense because they offer jobs and services; the urban share has risen from about 36 percent in 1950 to about 87 percent. Now the sparse areas. The Amazon is sparse because of dense forest that is hard to clear, heat and humidity, disease, poor access and leached latosol soils that fail quickly once cleared. The Centre-West was thinly settled because it was isolated, far from the coast and with few roads, before Brasília was built in 1960. The sertão is sparse because semi-arid rainfall of roughly 250 to 800 mm varies year to year, droughts destroy crops and the soils are thin and stony, so many people left. The contrast is clear: São Paulo state has about 180 people per km2 while Amazonas has under 3. Governments tried to move people inland. Brasília was inaugurated on 21 April 1960, the March to the West opened the interior, and the Trans-Amazonian Highway (1970s) and settlement of Rondônia along the BR-364 (1980s) tried to settle the Amazon. Many schemes failed because of poor soils and distance from markets, so the coast and the Southeast still hold most people.
